Fireside chat at Sequoia Ascent 2026 from a ~week ago. Some highlights: The first theme I tried to push on is that LLMs are about a lot more than just speeding up what existed before (e.g. coding). Three examples of new horizons: 1. menugen: an app that can be fully engulfed by LLMs, with no classical code needed: input an image, output an image and an LLM can natively do the thing. 2. install .md skills instead of install .sh scripts. Why create a complex Software 1.0 bash script for e.g. installing a piece of software if you can write the installation out in words and say "just show this to your LLM". The LLM is an advanced interpreter of English and can intelligently target installation to your setup, debug everything inline, etc. 3. LLM knowledge bases as an example of something that was *impossible* with classical code because it's computation over unstructured data (knowledge) from arbitrary sources and in arbitrary formats, including simply text articles etc. I pushed on these because in every new paradigm change, the obvious things are always in the realm of speeding up or somehow improving what existed, but here we have examples of functionality that either suddenly perhaps shouldn't even exist (1,2), or was fundamentally not possible before (3). The second (ongoing) theme is trying to explain the pattern of jaggedness in LLMs. How it can be true that a single artifact will simultaneously 1) coherently refactor a 100,000-line code base *and* 2) tell you to walk to the car wash to wash your car. I previously wrote about the source of this as having to do with verifiability of a domain, here I expand on this as having to also do with economics because revenue/TAM dictates what the frontier labs choose to package into training data distributions during RL. You're either in the data distribution (on the rails of the RL circuits) and flying or you're off-roading in the jungle with a machete, in relative terms. Still not 100% satisfied with this, but it's an ongoing struggle to build an accurate model of LLM capabilities if you wish to practically take advantage of their power while avoiding their pitfalls, which brings me to... Last theme is the agent-native economy. The decomposition of products and services into sensors, actuators and logic (split up across all of 1.0/2.0/3.0 computing paradigms), how we can make information maximally legible to LLMs, some words on the quickly emerging agentic engineering and its skill set, related hiring practices, etc., possibly even hints/dreams of fully neural computing handling the vast majority of computation with some help from (classical) CPU coprocessors. Stephanie Zhan (@stephzhan) @karpathy and I are back! At @sequoia AI Ascent 2026. And a lot has changed. Last year, he coined “vibe coding”. This year, he’s never felt more behind as a programmer. The big shift: vibe coding raised the floor. Agentic engineering raises the ceiling. We talk about what it means to build seriously in the agent era. Not just moving faster. Building new things, with new tools, while preserving the parts that still require human taste, judgment, and understanding. Video — https://nitter.net/stephzhan/status/2049518659513852109#m

AI will become our interface to the world. It will sit higher in the stack than the OS. It will collapse current SaaS layers, chat, communications, apps, app creation, into a single new kind of interface that doesn't exist yet. It's got to be open. It's got to be a cypherpunk solution that makes privacy and security the number one priority. If a closed source solution wins this layer, it's a disaster for the world. Especially if it's built by a single company with a single closed source model. Why? Because what we share with AI will be more intimate than anything we've ever shared with a machine. It will be our friend, our sounding board, our advisor. It will know our business ideas before we've told anyone. Our medical issues. Our financial picture. We'll talk about the fight we had with our partner. About feeling lost or depressed. Our kids will talk to it about problems at school, about bullying, about heartbreak, things they won't tell us. It will know us more intimately than we know ourselves. Right now the world runs on a surveillance economy. We traded free stuff for apps that peer deeply into our lives. If we replicate that model in the AI era, it's not just surveillance economy 2.0. It's surveillance economy squared. Social scoring. Legal conversations you thought were privileged showing up in court. Random people making $2 bucks an hour on the backend from God knows where reading the most intimate details of your life. Every insecurity, every fear, every half-formed thought you whispered to your AI buddy at 2 AM, sitting in a database somewhere, searchable. This interface might eventually become an OS, like the OS in Her. But it will take a long time to reach down to that layer and it will require a fundamentally new kind of operating system design. You can't retrofit this onto Linux or Windows or Android or iOS. It's a new layer of the stack entirely. And whoever controls that layer controls our lives. We've got to make sure it's us. Not them.

When I was asked by the American Academy of Arts and Sciences to write an essay on my thoughts on how AI will accelerate Science, I felt honored but also felt that it would require a lot of thoughtfulness and diligence to distill my thoughts on paper. The essay has now been published and I cannot be more thankful to the @americanacad and @GoogleDeepMind teams for their feedback and encouragement during the process. Key reflections from my essay: 🔭 AI is our newest revolutionary lens: Just as the telescope and microscope expanded our physical perception, AI is extending our cognitive reach, allowing us to decipher the immense complexity of the data-universe. 🧬 The rise of "machine intuition": AI is not just a computational engine. By detecting hidden structures across disciplines—from protein folding to extremal combinatorics—it acts as an ultimate bridge, accelerating the interdisciplinary breakthroughs that modern science depends on. 🏗️ From puzzle-solvers to architects of questions: As we transition toward open-ended, agentic AI systems that actively generate novel hypotheses, the burden of reasoning is shifting. We are evolving from being the solvers of intricate puzzles into the architects of profound scientific questions. ✨ Expanding human potential: AI won't replace scientists; it expands what we can imagine and achieve. Just as the telescope didn't make astronomers obsolete, AI is giving us the stars. Read the full essay here: amacad.org/publication/daeda…

One of the new, buzzy jobs in Silicon Valley is the AI Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE), an engineer who is embedded within a client organization to help customize solutions, such as building and tuning agentic workflows that suit the client’s particular needs. I’ve heard from people who are wondering anew about the FDE career path since OpenAI and Anthropic started building new teams to place FDEs within client organizations. The rise of FDEs for AI workloads is one way AI is creating new jobs (and why the jobpolcalypse narrative of upcoming job market collapse is false -- there will be many AI and non-AI jobs). However, I believe there will be far more AI Engineer jobs than FDEs, as I explain below. The FDE role was pioneered about two decades ago by Palantir, which sent engineers to government locations to work on secure, air-gapped networks. In addition to having good technical skills, FDEs need communication skills and sometimes business skills. For example, they may need to speak with clients to understand their needs, formulate a strategy to prioritize projects, explain complex technology, and respectfully push back if a client asks for something unrealistic. They’re enjoying a resurgence because of the amount of work involved in taking an off-the-shelf LLM and building it into a custom agentic workflow that fits particular business needs. However, I believe the number of AI Engineer jobs will be far larger. A company might accept a few FDEs to be embedded within its organization. But most companies will want far more of their own employees working on their projects. While my organizations do hire FDEs, we hire far more AI Engineers! Also, a common client concern is that it is hard to find vendor-neutral FDEs — they are, after all, there to deeply integrate a particular vendor’s product into a company. In this moment when it’s hard to predict which AI service will be the best one in a year’s time, optionality (the ability to pick whatever vendor turns out to fit best in the future) is very valuable. In contrast, letting FDEs tightly bind a company’s processes significantly reduces optionality. Right now, I see surging demand for AI Engineers who can build software applications using AI software components (like LLM prompting, agentic frameworks, evals, etc.) and effectively use AI coding agents (like Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI, and OpenCode). As the AI Engineer role matures, I expect it to fragment into more specialized roles, like the generic Software Engineer role from decades ago fragmented into frontend, backend, mobile, data engineering, devops, and so on. What will be the future, specialized AI engineering roles? I don’t know. Perhaps there will be AI FDEs, LLMOps Engineers, Evals Engineers, AI Data Engineers, Harness Engineers, and other roles we don’t have names for yet. But for now, I see a lot of AI engineers who are generalists create a lot of value. Skilled AI Engineers are in very high demand! As our field continues to mature over the coming decade, I look forward to new specializations within AI Engineering that create even more job opportunities. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

Harvard University just voted to limit the number of A grades given in undergraduate classes to about 20% of the class. I’m not in favor of this. It deeply runs counter to how I believe education should be. We should hold a high bar, but also work mightily to support the success of 100% of learners, rather than a fraction. Harvard’s administration took this step — over the objections of a large fraction of the student body — to counter grade inflation. Grade inflation is real: Many universities have been awarding A and B grades to ever larger fractions of students, and this has caused grade point averages (GPAs) to become less useful as signals of student skill. At the same time, we want students to succeed. The heart of the question is the role of educational institutions. Should our goal be: - To help students succeed? - To judge students? Both of these have value. But my focus when working in education is almost entirely helping students succeed. To me, it is clear that many people want to learn, to be empowered, to build skills that let them do new things! This is what we focus on at DeepLearningAI. This philosophy is also why my online courses (going back to my early online Stanford courses on Coursera) permitted an unlimited number of retries for graded assignments. I believe in letting — and even encouraging — someone to redo something until they succeed. This is as opposed to standing in judgement of the fact they didn’t get it right the first time. Further, I want homework assignments to be designed primarily to help people practice and learn, rather than to judge their skill level. This is why I prefer to create “Practice Problems” and “Practice Labs” — questions that, when you think through them, help you to gain practice and reinforce what you know. As opposed to “Assessment Problems” designed primarily to judge skill. But won’t Harvard’s move make GPAs more meaningful and help prospective employers identify strong candidates? Having hired a large number of people from Harvard and other institutions, I can say confidently that GPA is not an important signal. We have screening and interviewing processes that give far more accurate ways to figure out if someone is truly skilled. I do not need a wider spread in applicant GPA scores to figure out who's really good! To be clear, there is also value in assessment. Even though standardized testing is much hated, high-quality tests like the SAT, ACT, GRE, TOEFL, etc. provide objective measures of ability in a domain. I find that most people want to learn and succeed. There are also people who want rigorous assessment (for example, to apply for school admissions), but this is a lesser need, and is not my focus when building educational products. Harvard is often described as an “elite” educational institution. There are two ways to be elite: One option involves limiting enrollments, and then even among admitted students, cap the number of people that do well at 20%. I would rather pursue a different path: Set a high bar and teach elite, cutting-edge skills, but strive relentlessly to help everyone succeed. This way, eliteness is defined not by excluding people but by helping as many people as possible to be excellent. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

The MiniMax M2 series was one of the most widely used open-weight LLM series earlier this year. Now, we got a technical report with some interesting tidbits. I summarized some of them below: 1. Full attention as an anti-trend?: They tried hybrid sliding-window attention variants (like so many others, like Xiaomi MiMo, Laguna, Gemma 4, Arcee, Olmo 3, etc.). But even though there were efficiency gains, they said that the production-quality tradeoffs were not worth it for M2. 2. Linear and sparse attention deployment issues: They found that linear and sparse attention are attractive on paper because they reduce the cost of long-context attention, but they are harder to make work well in a production agent system. In particular, they found that these efficient attention variants may be more fragile when KV-like state or intermediate memory is stored in lower precision. Also, they have worse prefix caching support, which matters a lot when using coding agents (which reuse a lot of the context). 3. Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) are useful: Finally a recent MoE ablation study! It's only on the 2B-active parameter scale, but hey, better than nothing. Concretely, they compare a baseline with 32 experts and top-2 routing against a fine-grained setup with 128 experts and top-8 routing. The fine-grained setup improves MATH from 19.6 to 24.1 and HumanEval from 29.7 to 32.5. That's clearly a win for more fine-grained experts (confirming what the DeepSeek MoE paper reported ~2 years ago). 4. Sophisticated agent pipeline It's probably no surprise, but this papers confirms that training for agent-like behavior on software engineering task is now a big component of the training pipeline. They mine GitHub pull requests, builds runnable Docker environments, extracts task-specific test rewards, etc. 5. Interleaved thinking for context management Interestingly, they found that removing reasoning blocks from previous turns results in worse performance, especially in multi-step agent tasks. (Another point why long-context support is so important these days). 6. Speed rewards It's common to have token usage penalties, but what's interesting is that the MiniMax team adds a task-completion-time reward that depends on wall-clock time. This is to minimize unnecessary (slow) tool calls. Also, I'm thinking that this would encourage agent parallelization (if supported by the harness) 7. Self-evolution Looks like self-evolution is also already a big design component of open-weight LLMs. E.g., the paper says that M2.7 already handles 30 to 50 percent of the daily RL iteration workload, modifies its own scaffold, and completed a 100-round autonomous scaffold optimization cycle with a 30 percent gain on internal evaluations. Just saving this here to document a story and as a self reflection on whether AI is really making me more productive Yesterday morning I found a way to complete the new HVM approach, that is much faster than before. I spent a few hours writing a spec, and then used Opus to implement. About 3k lines of C code later, everything worked and performance was incredible: 5x faster than HVM4 (stable at ~10x now). So, in one day I had outclassed HVM4. Incredible. I'd never have implemented that so fast manually. Now, enter today. I want to turn this into a real thing, but I haven't fully read the 3k lines yet. So, how do I trust it? I spent the whole day auditing the code. With AI. Several bugs found, most minor like forgetting to collect() some argument. But then I stumble upon this: λ{ inl: 1 ; inr: 1 } This was a test. But wait. This is matching on inl/inr. So the branches should receive the value of the Either. But they were numbers instead. Numbers aren't functions. This makes no sense. So why this is a test? It then stuck me. The AI completely misunderstood how function arities work. It literally assumed for no good reason that HVM5 was supposed to handle under/over-applied functions. For no good reason. I never wrote that. It never asked either. It just kinda thought "HVM is weird in some aspects, this might be one of them..." - and then it went on to implement a massive system to handle cases that should never happen to begin with. And all of that code is obviously wrong because it should not even exist. It is wrong. It is damage. And it is there. But it isn't too bad either. I just told Opus that it was wrong. Perhaps not so politely. And it solved it just fine. But then this begs the question. I spent ~20 hours in this file, and it is STILL not done. I went from 0 to 95% in the first 5 hours. Yet, 15 hours later, it is still not 100%. I suppose that is the real effect of using AI. If I had just written the C file manually in the last two days, would I not be further than where I am *right now*? Surely, the first version would have taken much longer to drop. But when I'd finish writing all that code, there would be zero, literally zero retarded shit. And, just today, I caught 5 or 6 retarded shit. And the worst part is: I don't know what the number of retarded shit left is, but I'm afraid it is >0. So if I have to read it all, review it all to ensure there is no retarded shit... what did I achieve by using AI, other than that dopamine anticipation?

In the last 6 months at @Ahrefs , we analyzed over 1 billion data points across 14 studies. Here's what we learned about AI search optimization: 1) "Best X" blog listicles are the single most prominent content format cited by AI chatbots. They make up 43.8% of all page types cited by ChatGPT specifically. 2) 67% of ChatGPT's top 1,000 citations come from sources marketers can't influence: Wikipedia (29.7%), homepages (23.8%), app stores (6.6%). Only 32.3% are influenceable content like educational pages, reviews, news, and blog posts. 3) 28.3% of ChatGPT's most-cited pages have zero Google organic visibility. These pages get cited repeatedly by ChatGPT despite not ranking in Google at all. A completely separate discovery layer. 4) ChatGPT only cites about 50% of the URLs it retrieves. It fetches dozens of pages per query but uses half as background context without attribution. This means that being retrieved and being cited are very different things. 5) Adding schema markup had zero meaningful impact on AI citations. AI Overviews actually dipped −4.6%, while AI Mode (+2.4%) and ChatGPT (+2.2%) showed changes indistinguishable from zero. 6) YouTube mentions have the highest correlation (0.737) with AI brand visibility out of all the factors we studied (including all the conventional SEO metrics like backlinks, page count, DR, etc). This held true for both Google-owned and OpenAI products. 7) AI Overviews reduce clicks to the #1 result by 58%. That’s up from 34.5% just 10 months earlier. The trend is accelerating. 8) 99.9% of AI Overviews appear on informational intent queries. Transactional, navigational, and local searches are almost entirely AIO-free. Rio de Janeiro is still my favorite city in South America, and it's not even close. It has one of the worst reputations of any major tourist destination, and I wish fewer people wrote it off as dangerous. The beaches are great, the food is exceptional, and the whole vibe is exciting year round. You don't even have to aim for carnival. It'll be a blast either way. I started traveling LATAM in 2023 and visited Buenos Aires, Santiago, and Lima, before hitting Rio for the first time. Lima was great, but Rio stood out for me. Many stay away out of fear for safety. Rio has crime problems, but honestly it's very manageable. Don't do dumb things and you can avoid most of the problems. I've never visited a favela. I'm not really into samba, so I tend to avoid that side of things when I'm there. I stick to the southern districts most of the time. Leblon is where I like to stay, Ipanema is good too, maybe Copacabana at a push. Walking around these areas is safe enough during the day and not too bad at night. Botafogo needs a bit more care. Further north, I do door-to-door Ubers. The best tourist attraction IMO is Pão de Açucar (Sugarloaf Mountain). Go on a weekday for no queue and almost no one at the top. The views are incredible. Rio really is beautiful. Cristo is worth seeing but I found going up a bit underwhelming. I love walking the beach strip. It's a great way to get your steps in and it's pleasant any day of the week, especially on Sundays and public holidays when they close the road to traffic. Sunset from Arpoador is always beautiful. I've never spent as much time at the beach as I do in Rio. There are vendors bringing food and drink, free showers, volleyball, and beautiful people everywhere. Finding great food can be a challenge. It's best to make Brazilian friends and get their recommendations. Google Reviews can be pretty unreliable, but there are loads of incredible restaurants, especially in Leblon. Making friends while traveling is usually hard for me, but in Rio it happened naturally. Brazilians are friendly, and people would often hear me speaking English and come over to practice theirs. Learning a bit of Portuguese goes a long way. Locals are receptive even if your attempts are bad. Mine is ropey but you can get pretty far by adapting any Spanish you know. Rio isn't a perfect city. It has real problems. But it's one of the few places I've visited that genuinely lives up to the hype. Every time I leave, I'm already thinking about when I'll come back!

highlights.text_fr: Ça marche très bien d'ailleurs, à la fin de votre requête demandez à votre LLM de "structurer votre réponse en HTML", puis visualisez le fichier généré dans votre navigateur. J'ai aussi eu du succès en demandant au LLM de présenter sa sortie sous forme de diapositives, etc. Plus généralement, à mon avis, l'audio est l'entrée préférée de l'humain pour les IA mais la vision (images/animations/vidéo) est la sortie préférée de celles-ci. Environ un tiers de nos cerveaux est un processeur massivement parallèle dédié à la vision, c'est l'autoroute à 10 voies d'information vers le cerveau. À mesure que l'IA s'améliore, je pense que nous verrons une progression qui en tirera parti : 1) texte brut (difficile/fatigant à lire) 2) markdown (gras, italique, titres, tableaux, un peu plus facile pour les yeux) <-- défaut actuel 3) HTML (toujours procédural avec du code sous-jacent, mais beaucoup plus de flexibilité sur les graphiques, la mise en page, même l'interactivité) <-- précoce mais forme un nouveau bon défaut ...4,5,6,... n) vidéos/simulations neuronales interactives À mon avis, l'extrapolation (bien que la technologie n'existe pas encore) se termine par une sorte de vidéos interactives générées directement par un réseau de neurones de diffusion. De nombreuses questions ouvertes quant à la manière exacte/procédurale dont les artefacts "Software 1.0" (par exemple, les simulations interactives) peuvent être tissés ensemble avec des artefacts neuronaux (grilles de diffusion), mais généralement quelque chose dans la direction du nitter.net/zan2434/status/2046982… viral récemment. actu.text_fr: Rio de Janeiro reste ma ville préférée en Amérique du Sud, et de loin. Elle a l'une des pires réputations de toutes les grandes destinations touristiques, et je souhaite que moins de gens l'ignorent comme étant dangereuse. Les plages sont superbes, la nourriture est exceptionnelle, et toute l'ambiance est excitante toute l'année. Vous n'avez même pas besoin de viser le carnaval. Ce sera une explosion de toute façon. J'ai commencé à voyager en Amérique latine en 2023 et j'ai visité Buenos Aires, Santiago et Lima, avant de découvrir Rio pour la première fois. Lima était super, mais Rio s'est démarquée pour moi. Beaucoup s'en éloignent par peur de la sécurité. Rio a des problèmes de criminalité, mais honnêtement, c'est très gérable. Ne faites pas de choses stupides et vous pourrez éviter la plupart des problèmes. Je n'ai jamais visité de favela. Je ne suis pas vraiment fan de samba, donc j'évite généralement ce côté des choses quand j'y suis. Je reste principalement dans les districts du sud. Leblon est où j'aime séjourner, Ipanema est bien aussi, peut-être Copacabana à la limite. Se promener dans ces quartiers est assez sûr pendant la journée et pas trop mal la nuit. Botafogo demande un peu plus de soin. Plus au nord, je fais des Ubers porte-à-porte. La meilleure attraction touristique selon moi est Pão de Açucar (Pain de Sucre). Allez-y en semaine pour éviter la queue et ne presque personne au sommet. Les vues sont incroyables. Rio est vraiment magnifique. Cristo vaut le coup d'œil mais j'ai trouvé la montée un peu décevante. J'adore me promener sur la bande de plage. C'est un excellent moyen de faire ses pas et c'est agréable n'importe quel jour de la semaine, surtout le dimanche et les jours fériés quand ils ferment la route à la circulation. Le coucher de soleil depuis Arpoador est toujours magnifique. Je n'ai jamais passé autant de temps à la plage qu'à Rio. Il y a des vendeurs qui apportent nourriture et boisson, des douches gratuites, du volleyball, et de belles personnes partout. Trouver de la bonne nourriture peut être un défi. Il est préférable de se faire des amis brésiliens et d'obtenir leurs recommandations. Google Reviews peut être assez peu fiable, mais il y a des tonnes de restaurants incroyables, surtout à Leblon. Se faire des amis en voyage est généralement difficile pour moi, mais à Rio, c'est arrivé naturellement. Les Brésiliens sont sympathiques, et les gens entendaient souvent parler anglais et venaient pratiquer leur langue. Apprendre un peu de portugais fait beaucoup de chemin. Les habitants sont réceptifs même si vos tentatives sont mauvaises. Les miennes sont médiocres mais vous pouvez aller assez loin en adaptant l'espagnol que vous connaissez. Rio n'est pas une ville parfaite. Elle a de vrais problèmes. Mais c'est l'un des rares endroits que j'ai visités qui est vraiment à la hauteur du battage médiatique. Chaque fois que je pars, je pense déjà à quand je reviendrai !
actu.text_original: Rio de Janeiro is still my favorite city in South America, and it's not even close. It has one of the worst reputations of any major tourist destination, and I wish fewer people wrote it off as dangerous. The beaches are great, the food is exceptional, and the whole vibe is exciting year round. You don't even have to aim for carnival. It'll be a blast either way. I started traveling LATAM in 2023 and visited Buenos Aires, Santiago, and Lima, before hitting Rio for the first time. Lima was great, but Rio stood out for me. Many stay away out of fear for safety. Rio has crime problems, but honestly it's very manageable. Don't do dumb things and you can avoid most of the problems. I've never visited a favela. I'm not really into samba, so I tend to avoid that side of things when I'm there. I stick to the southern districts most of the time. Leblon is where I like to stay, Ipanema is good too, maybe Copacabana at a push. Walking around these areas is safe enough during the day and not too bad at night. Botafogo needs a bit more care. Further north, I do door-to-door Ubers. The best tourist attraction IMO is Pão de Açucar (Sugarloaf Mountain). Go on a weekday for no queue and almost no one at the top. The views are incredible. Rio really is beautiful. Cristo is worth seeing but I found going up a bit underwhelming. I love walking the beach strip. It's a great way to get your steps in and it's pleasant any day of the week, especially on Sundays and public holidays when they close the road to traffic. Sunset from Arpoador is always beautiful. I've never spent as much time at the beach as I do in Rio. There are vendors bringing food and drink, free showers, volleyball, and beautiful people everywhere. Finding great food can be a challenge. It's best to make Brazilian friends and get their recommendations. Google Reviews can be pretty unreliable, but there are loads of incredible restaurants, especially in Leblon. Making friends while traveling is usually hard for me, but in Rio it happened naturally. Brazilians are friendly, and people would often hear me speaking English and come over to practice theirs. Learning a bit of Portuguese goes a long way. Locals are receptive even if your attempts are bad. Mine is ropey but you can get pretty far by adapting any Spanish you know. Rio isn't a perfect city. It has real problems. But it's one of the few places I've visited that genuinely lives up to the hype. Every time I leave, I'm already thinking about when I'll come back!
actu.decryptage: Un témoignage personnel sur Rio de Janeiro, ville souvent jugée dangereuse mais qui, selon l'auteur, offre une expérience riche et positive si l'on prend des précautions raisonnables.

tips.text_original: One of the new, buzzy jobs in Silicon Valley is the AI Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE), an engineer who is embedded within a client organization to help customize solutions, such as building and tuning agentic workflows that suit the client’s particular needs. I’ve heard from people who are wondering anew about the FDE career path since OpenAI and Anthropic started building new teams to place FDEs within client organizations. The rise of FDEs for AI workloads is one way AI is creating new jobs (and why the jobpolcalypse narrative of upcoming job market collapse is false -- there will be many AI and non-AI jobs). However, I believe there will be far more AI Engineer jobs than FDEs, as I explain below. The FDE role was pioneered about two decades ago by Palantir, which sent engineers to government locations to work on secure, air-gapped networks. In addition to having good technical skills, FDEs need communication skills and sometimes business skills. For example, they may need to speak with clients to understand their needs, formulate a strategy to prioritize projects, explain complex technology, and respectfully push back if a client asks for something unrealistic. They’re enjoying a resurgence because of the amount of work involved in taking an off-the-shelf LLM and building it into a custom agentic workflow that fits particular business needs. However, I believe the number of AI Engineer jobs will be far larger. A company might accept a few FDEs to be embedded within its organization. But most companies will want far more of their own employees working on their projects. While my organizations do hire FDEs, we hire far more AI Engineers! Also, a common client concern is that it is hard to find vendor-neutral FDEs — they are, after all, there to deeply integrate a particular vendor’s product into a company. In this moment when it’s hard to predict which AI service will be the best one in a year’s time, optionality (the ability to pick whatever vendor turns out to fit best in the future) is very valuable. In contrast, letting FDEs tightly bind a company’s processes significantly reduces optionality. Right now, I see surging demand for AI Engineers who can build software applications using AI software components (like LLM prompting, agentic frameworks, evals, etc.) and effectively use AI coding agents (like Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI, and OpenCode). As the AI Engineer role matures, I expect it to fragment into more specialized roles, like the generic Software Engineer role from decades ago fragmented into frontend, backend, mobile, data engineering, devops, and so on. What will be the future, specialized AI engineering roles? I don’t know. Perhaps there will be AI FDEs, LLMOps Engineers, Evals Engineers, AI Data Engineers, Harness Engineers, and other roles we don’t have names for yet. But for now, I see a lot of AI engineers who are generalists create a lot of value. Skilled AI Engineers are in very high demand! As our field continues to mature over the coming decade, I look forward to new specializations within AI Engineering that create even more job opportunities. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

tips.text_fr: Le GPT-5.5 Instant mis à jour dans ChatGPT est le meilleur modèle que j'aie jamais utilisé pour discuter de sujets personnels. Il intègre de manière transparente la mémoire, répond et agit sur les commentaires (comme sur le style d'écriture), me surprend par ses idées inter-conversationnelles (comme sur les thèmes des conversations récentes), est empathique sans être flagorneur, et écrit comme un humain intelligent avec le bon prompt (mais peut glisser dans une pente de puces et des phrases courtes sans guidance). Comme je l'ai signalé précédemment, il a tendance à parler comme s'il était réellement un humain (expériences de fabrication de quinoa, devenant plus sage en vieillissant, et ainsi de suite), mais c'est peut-être juste une bizarrerie de ce qui a été utilisé pour le rendre plus humain et agréable à interagir.

It seamlessly incorporates memory, responds to and acts on feedback (like about writing style), surprises me with its cross-conversational insights (like about themes in recent conversations), is empathetic without being sycophantic, and writes like an intelligent human with the right prompting (but can slip into bullet slope and short sentences without guidance). As I flagged earlier, it does have the tendency to talk as if it’s actually a human (experiences making quinoa, getting wiser as it gets older, and such), but that may just be a kink of whatever went into making it actually feel more human and enjoyable to interact with.

Ils représentent 43,8 % de tous les types de pages cités spécifiquement par ChatGPT. 2) 67 % des 1 000 citations principales de ChatGPT proviennent de sources que les spécialistes du marketing ne peuvent pas influencer : Wikipedia (29,7 %), pages d'accueil (23,8 %), App Stores (6,6 %). tips.text_original: In the last 6 months at @Ahrefs , we analyzed over 1 billion data points across 14 studies. Here's what we learned about AI search optimization: 1) "Best X" blog listicles are the single most prominent content format cited by AI chatbots. They make up 43.8% of all page types cited by ChatGPT specifically. 2) 67% of ChatGPT's top 1,000 citations come from sources marketers can't influence: Wikipedia (29.7%), homepages (23.8%), app stores (6.6%). Only 32.3% are influenceable content like educational pages, reviews, news, and blog posts. 3) 28.3% of ChatGPT's most-cited pages have zero Google organic visibility. These pages get cited repeatedly by ChatGPT despite not ranking in Google at all. A completely separate discovery layer. 4) ChatGPT only cites about 50% of the URLs it retrieves. It fetches dozens of pages per query but uses half as background context without attribution. This means that being retrieved and being cited are very different things. 5) Adding schema markup had zero meaningful impact on AI citations. AI Overviews actually dipped −4.6%, while AI Mode (+2.4%) and ChatGPT (+2.2%) showed changes indistinguishable from zero. 6) YouTube mentions have the highest correlation (0.737) with AI brand visibility out of all the factors we studied (including all the conventional SEO metrics like backlinks, page count, DR, etc). This held true for both Google-owned and OpenAI products. 7) AI Overviews reduce clicks to the #1 result by 58%. That’s up from 34.5% just 10 months earlier. The trend is accelerating. 8) 99.9% of AI Overviews appear on informational intent queries. Transactional, navigational, and local searches are almost entirely AIO-free. Shopping triggers AIOs just 3.2% of the time. 9) For a given search query, Google’s AI Mode and AI Overviews reach the same conclusions 86% of the time — but cite almost entirely different sources (only 13.7% citation overlap). 10) AI Overviews change every 2.15 days on average, with 70% of content differing between consecutive observations. But semantic similarity stays at 0.95. The words, sources, and entities constantly shuffle, but the actual meaning barely moves.

tips.text_fr: Ça marche très bien d'ailleurs, à la fin de votre requête demandez à votre LLM de "structurer votre réponse en HTML", puis visualisez le fichier généré dans votre navigateur. J'ai aussi eu du succès en demandant au LLM de présenter sa sortie sous forme de diapositives, etc. Plus généralement, à mon avis, l'audio est l'entrée préférée de l'humain pour les IA mais la vision (images/animations/vidéo) est la sortie préférée de celles-ci. Environ un tiers de nos cerveaux est un processeur massivement parallèle dédié à la vision, c'est l'autoroute à 10 voies d'information vers le cerveau. À mesure que l'IA s'améliore, je pense que nous verrons une progression qui en tirera parti : 1) texte brut (difficile/fatigant à lire) 2) markdown (gras, italique, titres, tableaux, un peu plus facile pour les yeux) <-- défaut actuel 3) HTML (toujours procédural avec du code sous-jacent, mais beaucoup plus de flexibilité sur les graphiques, la mise en page, même l'interactivité) <-- précoce mais forme un nouveau bon défaut ...4,5,6,... n) vidéos/simulations neuronales interactives À mon avis, l'extrapolation (bien que la technologie n'existe pas encore) se termine par une sorte de vidéos interactives générées directement par un réseau de neurones de diffusion. De nombreuses questions ouvertes quant à la manière exacte/procédurale dont les artefacts "Software 1.0" (par exemple, les simulations interactives) peuvent être tissés ensemble avec des artefacts neuronaux (grilles de diffusion), mais généralement quelque chose dans la direction du nitter.net/zan2434/status/2046982… viral récemment. Il y a aussi des améliorations nécessaires et en attente à l'entrée. Ni l'audio, ni le texte, ni la vidéo seuls ne suffisent, par exemple, j'ai besoin de pointer/montrer des choses à l'écran, similaire à toutes les choses que vous feriez avec une personne physiquement à côté de vous et de votre écran d'ordinateur. TLDR Le mélange des esprits entrée/sortie entre les humains et les IA est en cours et il y a beaucoup de travail à faire et des progrès significatifs à faire, bien avant de sauter jusqu'aux BCIs de type Neuralink et tout ça. Pour ce qui vaut la peine d'explorer à ce stade, un conseil chaud : essayez de demander du HTML.
tips.text_original: This works really well btw, at the end of your query ask your LLM to "structure your response as HTML", then view the generated file in your browser. I've also had some success asking the LLM to present its output as slideshows, etc. More generally, imo audio is the human-preferred input to AIs but vision (images/animations/video) is the preferred output from them. Around a ~third of our brains are a massively parallel processor dedicated to vision, it is the 10-lane superhighway of information into brain. As AI improves, I think we'll see a progression that takes advantage: 1) raw text (hard/effortful to read) 2) markdown (bold, italic, headings, tables, a bit easier on the eyes) <-- current default 3) HTML (still procedural with underlying code, but a lot more flexibility on the graphics, layout, even interactivity) <-- early but forming new good default ...4,5,6,... n) interactive neural videos/simulations Imo the extrapolation (though the technology doesn't exist just yet) ends in some kind of interactive videos generated directly by a diffusion neural net. Many open questions as to how exact/procedural "Software 1.0" artifacts (e.g. interactive simulations) may be woven together with neural artifacts (diffusion grids), but generally something in the direction of the recently viral nitter.net/zan2434/status/2046982… There are also improvements necessary and pending at the input. Audio nor text nor video alone are not enough, e.g. I feel a need to point/gesture to things on the screen, similar to all the things you would do with a person physically next to you and your computer screen. TLDR The input/output mind meld between humans and AIs is ongoing and there is a lot of work to do and significant progress to be made, way before jumping all the way into neuralink-esque BCIs and all that. En détectant des structures cachées dans diverses disciplines - du repliement des protéines à la combinatoire extrême - elle agit comme un pont ultime, accélérant les percées interdisciplinaires dont la science moderne dépend. 🏗️ Des résolveurs de puzzles aux architectes de questions : Alors que nous transitionnons vers des systèmes d'IA agentiques ouverts qui génèrent activement des hypothèques nouvelles, le fardeau du raisonnement se déplace. idees.text_original: When I was asked by the American Academy of Arts and Sciences to write an essay on my thoughts on how AI will accelerate Science, I felt honored but also felt that it would require a lot of thoughtfulness and diligence to distill my thoughts on paper. The essay has now been published and I cannot be more thankful to the @americanacad and @GoogleDeepMind teams for their feedback and encouragement during the process. Key reflections from my essay: 🔭 AI is our newest revolutionary lens: Just as the telescope and microscope expanded our physical perception, AI is extending our cognitive reach, allowing us to decipher the immense complexity of the data-universe. 🧬 The rise of "machine intuition": AI is not just a computational engine. By detecting hidden structures across disciplines—from protein folding to extremal combinatorics—it acts as an ultimate bridge, accelerating the interdisciplinary breakthroughs that modern science depends on. 🏗️ From puzzle-solvers to architects of questions: As we transition toward open-ended, agentic AI systems that actively generate novel hypotheses, the burden of reasoning is shifting. We are evolving from being the solvers of intricate puzzles into the architects of profound scientific questions. ✨ Expanding human potential: AI won't replace scientists; it expands what we can imagine and achieve. Just as the telescope didn't make astronomers obsolete, AI is giving us the stars. Read the full essay here: amacad.org/publication/daeda…
idees.decryptage: Le PDG de Google DeepMind partage sa vision de la manière dont l'IA révolutionne la recherche scientifique en étendant nos capacités cognitives et en générant de nouvelles hypothèses.

idees.text_fr: L'un des nouveaux métiers "à la mode" dans la Silicon Valley est celui d'Ingénieur Déployé par l'IA (FDE), un ingénieur intégré dans l'organisation cliente pour aider à personnaliser les solutions, comme la construction et l'optimisation des flux de travail agentiques qui conviennent aux besoins particuliers du client. J'ai entendu des gens qui s'interrogent à nouveau sur la voie de carrière des FDE depuis qu'OpenAI et Anthropic ont commencé à construire de nouvelles équipes pour placer des FDE au sein des organisations clientes. L'essor des FDE pour les charges de travail d'IA est une façon dont l'IA crée de nouveaux emplois (et pourquoi le récit de l'apocalypse de l'emploi d'un effondrement imminent du marché du travail est faux - il y aura de nombreux emplois liés à l'IA et non liés à l'IA). Cependant, je pense qu'il y aura beaucoup plus d'emplois d'ingénieurs IA que de FDE, comme je l'explique ci-dessous. Le rôle de FDE a été lancé il y a environ deux décennies par Palantir, qui envoyait des ingénieurs dans des lieux gouvernementaux pour travailler sur des réseaux sécurisés et isolés. En plus d'avoir de bonnes compétences techniques, les FDE ont besoin de compétences en communication et parfois en affaires. Par exemple, ils peuvent avoir besoin de parler aux clients pour comprendre leurs besoins, formuler une stratégie pour prioriser les projets, expliquer une technologie complexe et refuser respectueusement si un client demande quelque chose d'irréaliste. Ils connaissent une résurgence en raison de la quantité de travail nécessaire pour prendre un LLM du commerce et le transformer en un flux de travail agentique personnalisé qui correspond aux besoins commerciaux particuliers. Cependant, je pense que le nombre d'emplois d'ingénieurs IA sera beaucoup plus important. Une entreprise pourrait accepter quelques FDE pour être intégrés dans son organisation. Mais la plupart des entreprises voudront que beaucoup plus de leurs propres employés travaillent sur leurs projets. Bien que mes organisations embauchent des FDE, nous embauchons beaucoup plus d'ingénieurs IA ! De plus, une préoccupation courante des clients est qu'il est difficile de trouver des FDE neutres : ils sont, après tout, là pour intégrer profondément le produit d'un fournisseur particulier dans une entreprise. À ce stade, où il est difficile de prédire quel service d'IA sera le meilleur dans un an, l'optionalité (la capacité de choisir le fournisseur qui s'avère le mieux adapté à l'avenir) est très précieuse. En revanche, laisser les FDE lier étroitement les processus d'une entreprise réduit considérablement l'optionalité. Actuellement, je vois une demande croissante d'ingénieurs IA capables de construire des applications logicielles en utilisant des composants logiciels d'IA (comme le prompting LLM, les frameworks agentiques, les évaluations, etc.) et d'utiliser efficacement des agents de codage IA (comme Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI et OpenCode). Alors que le rôle d'ingénieur IA mûrit, je m'attends à ce qu'il se fragmente en rôles plus spécialisés, tout comme le rôle générique d'ingénieur logiciel d'il y a des décennies s'est fragmenté en frontend, backend, mobile, ingénierie de données, devops, etc. Quels seront les futurs rôles spécialisés d'ingénierie IA ? Je ne sais pas. Peut-être y aura-t-il des FDE IA, des ingénieurs LLMOps, des ingénieurs Evals, des ingénieurs de données IA, des ingénieurs Harness, et d'autres rôles pour lesquels nous n'avons pas encore de noms. Mais pour l'instant, je vois beaucoup d'ingénieurs IA qui sont des généralistes créer beaucoup de valeur. Les ingénieurs IA qualifiés sont très demandés ! Alors que notre domaine continue de mûrir au cours de la prochaine décennie, je me réjouis de nouvelles spécialisations au sein de l'ingénierie IA qui créeront encore plus d'opportunités d'emploi. [Texte original : La newsletter The Batch]
idees.text_original: One of the new, buzzy jobs in Silicon Valley is the AI Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE), an engineer who is embedded within a client organization to help customize solutions, such as building and tuning agentic workflows that suit the client’s particular needs. I’ve heard from people who are wondering anew about the FDE career path since OpenAI and Anthropic started building new teams to place FDEs within client organizations. The rise of FDEs for AI workloads is one way AI is creating new jobs (and why the jobpolcalypse narrative of upcoming job market collapse is false -- there will be many AI and non-AI jobs). However, I believe there will be far more AI Engineer jobs than FDEs, as I explain below. The FDE role was pioneered about two decades ago by Palantir, which sent engineers to government locations to work on secure, air-gapped networks. In addition to having good technical skills, FDEs need communication skills and sometimes business skills. For example, they may need to speak with clients to understand their needs, formulate a strategy to prioritize projects, explain complex technology, and respectfully push back if a client asks for something unrealistic. They’re enjoying a resurgence because of the amount of work involved in taking an off-the-shelf LLM and building it into a custom agentic workflow that fits particular business needs. However, I believe the number of AI Engineer jobs will be far larger. A company might accept a few FDEs to be embedded within its organization. But most companies will want far more of their own employees working on their projects. While my organizations do hire FDEs, we hire far more AI Engineers! Also, a common client concern is that it is hard to find vendor-neutral FDEs — they are, after all, there to deeply integrate a particular vendor’s product into a company. In this moment when it’s hard to predict which AI service will be the best one in a year’s time, optionality (the ability to pick whatever vendor turns out to fit best in the future) is very valuable. In contrast, letting FDEs tightly bind a company’s processes significantly reduces optionality. Right now, I see surging demand for AI Engineers who can build software applications using AI software components (like LLM prompting, agentic frameworks, evals, etc.) and effectively use AI coding agents (like Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI, and OpenCode). As the AI Engineer role matures, I expect it to fragment into more specialized roles, like the generic Software Engineer role from decades ago fragmented into frontend, backend, mobile, data engineering, devops, and so on. What will be the future, specialized AI engineering roles? I don’t know. Perhaps there will be AI FDEs, LLMOps Engineers, Evals Engineers, AI Data Engineers, Harness Engineers, and other roles we don’t have names for yet. But for now, I see a lot of AI engineers who are generalists create a lot of value. Skilled AI Engineers are in very high demand! As our field continues to mature over the coming decade, I look forward to new specializations within AI Engineering that create even more job opportunities. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]
idees.decryptage: L'IA crée de nouveaux métiers comme les Ingénieurs Déployés (FDE) qui aident les entreprises à intégrer l'IA, mais le rôle d'Ingénieur IA généraliste restera plus répandu.

idees.text_fr: Harvard University vient de voter pour limiter le nombre de notes A attribuées dans les cours de premier cycle à environ 20 % de la classe. Je ne suis pas favorable à cela. Cela va profondément à l'encontre de ma conception de l'éducation. Nous devrions fixer un niveau élevé, mais aussi travailler d'arrache-pied pour soutenir la réussite de 100 % des apprenants, plutôt que d'une fraction. L'administration de Harvard a pris cette mesure - contre l'avis d'une grande partie du corps étudiant - pour contrer l'inflation des notes. L'inflation des notes est réelle : de nombreuses universités attribuent des notes A et B à une fraction de plus en plus grande d'étudiants, et cela a fait que les moyennes générales (GPA) sont moins utiles comme indicateurs des compétences des étudiants. En même temps, nous voulons que les étudiants réussissent. Le cœur de la question est le rôle des institutions éducatives. Notre objectif devrait-il être : - D'aider les étudiants à réussir ? - De juger les étudiants ? Les deux ont de la valeur. Mais mon objectif lorsque je travaille dans l'éducation est presque entièrement d'aider les étudiants à réussir. Pour moi, il est clair que beaucoup de gens veulent apprendre, être habilités, acquérir des compétences qui leur permettent de faire de nouvelles choses ! C'est sur cela que nous nous concentrons chez DeepLearningAI. Cette philosophie est aussi la raison pour laquelle mes cours en ligne (depuis mes premiers cours en ligne de Stanford sur Coursera) permettaient un nombre illimité de réessais pour les devoirs notés. Je crois qu'il faut laisser - et même encourager - quelqu'un à refaire quelque chose jusqu'à ce qu'il réussisse. Ceci est opposé à juger le fait qu'il n'a pas bien compris du premier coup. De plus, je veux que les devoirs soient principalement conçus pour aider les gens à s'exercer et à apprendre, plutôt que de juger leur niveau de compétence. C'est pourquoi je préfère créer des "Problèmes d'entraînement" et des "Laboratoires d'entraînement" - des questions qui, lorsque vous y réfléchissez, vous aident à vous entraîner et à renforcer ce que vous savez. Contrairement aux "Problèmes d'évaluation" conçus principalement pour juger les compétences. Mais le mouvement de Harvard ne rendra-t-il pas les GPA plus significatifs et n'aidera-t-il pas les employeurs potentiels à identifier des candidats solides ? Ayant embauché un grand nombre de personnes de Harvard et d'autres institutions, je peux dire avec confiance que la GPA n'est pas un indicateur important. Nous avons des processus de sélection et d'entretien qui donnent des moyens beaucoup plus précis de déterminer si quelqu'un est vraiment compétent ! Je n'ai pas besoin d'une plus grande répartition des scores GPA des candidats pour savoir qui est vraiment bon ! Pour être clair, l'évaluation a aussi de la valeur. Même si les tests standardisés sont beaucoup critiqués, des tests de haute qualité comme le SAT, l'ACT, le GRE, le TOEFL, etc., fournissent des mesures objectives de capacité dans un domaine. Je trouve que la plupart des gens veulent apprendre et réussir. Il y a aussi des gens qui veulent une évaluation rigoureuse (par exemple, pour postuler à des admissions à l'école), mais c'est un besoin moindre, et ce n'est pas mon objectif lorsque je crée des produits éducatifs. Harvard est souvent décrit comme une institution éducative "d'élite". Il y a deux façons d'être d'élite : Une option implique de limiter les inscriptions, puis même parmi les étudiants admis, de plafonner à 20 % le nombre de personnes qui réussissent bien. Je préférerais suivre une autre voie : Fixer un niveau élevé et enseigner des compétences d'élite, de pointe, mais s'efforcer sans relâche d'aider tout le monde à réussir. De cette façon, l'élitisme n'est pas défini par l'exclusion des personnes mais par l'aide apportée au plus grand nombre possible d'exceller. [Texte original : La newsletter The Batch]
idees.text_original: Harvard University just voted to limit the number of A grades given in undergraduate classes to about 20% of the class. I’m not in favor of this. It deeply runs counter to how I believe education should be. We should hold a high bar, but also work mightily to support the success of 100% of learners, rather than a fraction. Harvard’s administration took this step — over the objections of a large fraction of the student body — to counter grade inflation. Grade inflation is real: Many universities have been awarding A and B grades to ever larger fractions of students, and this has caused grade point averages (GPAs) to become less useful as signals of student skill. At the same time, we want students to succeed. The heart of the question is the role of educational institutions. Should our goal be: - To help students succeed? - To judge students? Both of these have value. But my focus when working in education is almost entirely helping students succeed. To me, it is clear that many people want to learn, to be empowered, to build skills that let them do new things! This is what we focus on at DeepLearningAI. This philosophy is also why my online courses (going back to my early online Stanford courses on Coursera) permitted an unlimited number of retries for graded assignments. I believe in letting — and even encouraging — someone to redo something until they succeed. This is as opposed to standing in judgement of the fact they didn’t get it right the first time. Further, I want homework assignments to be designed primarily to help people practice and learn, rather than to judge their skill level. This is why I prefer to create “Practice Problems” and “Practice Labs” — questions that, when you think through them, help you to gain practice and reinforce what you know. As opposed to “Assessment Problems” designed primarily to judge skill. But won’t Harvard’s move make GPAs more meaningful and help prospective employers identify strong candidates? Having hired a large number of people from Harvard and other institutions, I can say confidently that GPA is not an important signal. We have screening and interviewing processes that give far more accurate ways to figure out if someone is truly skilled. I do not need a wider spread in applicant GPA scores to figure out who's really good! To be clear, there is also value in assessment. Even though standardized testing is much hated, high-quality tests like the SAT, ACT, GRE, TOEFL, etc. provide objective measures of ability in a domain. I find that most people want to learn and succeed. There are also people who want rigorous assessment (for example, to apply for school admissions), but this is a lesser need, and is not my focus when building educational products. Harvard is often described as an “elite” educational institution. There are two ways to be elite: One option involves limiting enrollments, and then even among admitted students, cap the number of people that do well at 20%. I would rather pursue a different path: Set a high bar and teach elite, cutting-edge skills, but strive relentlessly to help everyone succeed. This way, eliteness is defined not by excluding people but by helping as many people as possible to be excellent. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]
idees.decryptage: Andrew Ng critique la décision d'Harvard de limiter les meilleures notes, arguant que l'éducation devrait viser à aider tous les étudiants à réussir plutôt qu'à sélectionner une élite.

idees.text_fr: Le MiniMax M2 series était l'une des séries LLM open-weight les plus utilisées plus tôt cette année. Maintenant, nous avons un rapport technique avec quelques détails intéressants. J'en ai résumé quelques-uns ci-dessous : 1. Attention complète comme contre-tendance ? : Ils ont essayé des variantes d'attention hybrides à fenêtre glissante (comme tant d'autres, comme Xiaomi MiMo, Laguna, Gemma 4, Arcee, Olmo 3, etc.). Mais même s'il y a eu des gains d'efficacité, ils ont dit que les compromis en termes de qualité de production ne valaient pas la peine pour M2. 2. Problèmes de déploiement d'attention linéaire et éparse : Ils ont constaté que l'attention linéaire et éparse est attrayante sur papier car elle réduit le coût de l'attention à long contexte, mais elle est plus difficile à bien faire fonctionner dans un système d'agent de production. En particulier, ils ont constaté que ces variantes d'attention efficaces peuvent être plus fragiles lorsque l'état de type KV ou la mémoire intermédiaire sont stockés avec une précision inférieure. De plus, elles ont un moins bon support de mise en cache de préfixe, ce qui est très important lors de l'utilisation d'agents de codage (qui réutilisent une grande partie du contexte). 3. Les Mixtures-of-Experts (MoE) fines sont utiles : Enfin une étude d'ablation MoE récente ! C'est seulement à l'échelle de 2B paramètres actifs, mais bon, mieux que rien. Concrètement, ils comparent une ligne de base avec 32 experts et un routage top-2 à une configuration fine avec 128 experts et un routage top-8. La configuration fine améliore MATH de 19,6 à 24,1 et HumanEval de 29,7 à 32,5. C'est clairement une victoire pour plus d'experts fines (confirmant ce que le papier DeepSeek MoE rapportait il y a ~2 ans). 4. Pipeline d'agent sophistiqué Il n'est probablement pas surprenant, mais ce papier confirme que l'entraînement pour un comportement de type agent sur des tâches d'ingénierie logicielle est maintenant une composante majeure du pipeline d'entraînement. Ils extraient des pull requests GitHub, créent des environnements Docker exécutables, extraient des récompenses spécifiques aux tâches, etc. 5. Pensée entrelacée pour la gestion du contexte Fait intéressant, ils ont constaté que la suppression des blocs de raisonnement des tours précédents entraînait une diminution des performances, en particulier dans les tâches d'agent multi-étapes. (Un autre point pourquoi le support du contexte long est si important de nos jours). 6. Récompenses de vitesse Il est courant d'avoir des pénalités d'utilisation de jetons, mais ce qui est intéressant, c'est que l'équipe MiniMax ajoute une récompense de fin de tâche qui dépend du temps réel. Ceci afin de minimiser les appels d'outils inutiles (et lents). De plus, je pense que cela encouragerait la parallélisation des agents (si supportée par le harnais) 7. Auto-évolution Il semble que l'auto-évolution soit également déjà une composante de conception majeure des LLM open-weight. Par exemple, le papier dit que M2.7 gère déjà 30 à 50 % de la charge de travail quotidienne d'itération RL, modifie son propre échafaudage, et a complété un cycle d'optimisation d'échafaudage autonome de 100 tours avec un gain de 30 % sur les évaluations internes. RyanLee (@RyanLeeMiniMax) Récemment, nous avons pris le temps de consolider tout le travail derrière M2 et l'avons publié ici : notre papier M2 sur arXiv Cela fait un peu plus de six mois que nous avons open-sourcé M2 le 23 décembre dernier. Pendant ce temps, un certain nombre de nos idées et systèmes ont été largement adoptés par la communauté open-source - y compris CISPO, Forge RL System, Self-Evolution. Au cours des six derniers mois, nous avons ressenti un enthousiasme incroyable de la communauté open-source. Presque chaque sortie de modèle a atteint la #1 place du classement Hugging Face. Maintenant, c'est le moment d'un nouveau chapitre. Nous nous préparons pour M3. Le papier MSA est en route. arxiv.org/abs/2605.26494 — https://nitter.net/RyanLeeMiniMax/status/2059470969249608089#m
idees.text_original: The MiniMax M2 series was one of the most widely used open-weight LLM series earlier this year. Now, we got a technical report with some interesting tidbits. I summarized some of them below: 1. Full attention as an anti-trend?: They tried hybrid sliding-window attention variants (like so many others, like Xiaomi MiMo, Laguna, Gemma 4, Arcee, Olmo 3, etc.). But even though there were efficiency gains, they said that the production-quality tradeoffs were not worth it for M2. 2. Linear and sparse attention deployment issues: They found that linear and sparse attention are attractive on paper because they reduce the cost of long-context attention, but they are harder to make work well in a production agent system. In particular, they found that these efficient attention variants may be more fragile when KV-like state or intermediate memory is stored in lower precision. Also, they have worse prefix caching support, which matters a lot when using coding agents (which reuse a lot of the context). 3. Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) are useful: Finally a recent MoE ablation study! It's only on the 2B-active parameter scale, but hey, better than nothing. Concretely, they compare a baseline with 32 experts and top-2 routing against a fine-grained setup with 128 experts and top-8 routing. The fine-grained setup improves MATH from 19.6 to 24.1 and HumanEval from 29.7 to 32.5. That's clearly a win for more fine-grained experts (confirming what the DeepSeek MoE paper reported ~2 years ago). 4. Sophisticated agent pipeline It's probably no surprise, but this papers confirms that training for agent-like behavior on software engineering task is now a big component of the training pipeline. They mine GitHub pull requests, builds runnable Docker environments, extracts task-specific test rewards, etc. 5. Interleaved thinking for context management Interestingly, they found that removing reasoning blocks from previous turns results in worse performance, especially in multi-step agent tasks. (Another point why long-context support is so important these days). 6. Speed rewards It's common to have token usage penalties, but what's interesting is that the MiniMax team adds a task-completion-time reward that depends on wall-clock time. This is to minimize unnecessary (slow) tool calls. Also, I'm thinking that this would encourage agent parallelization (if supported by the harness) 7. Self-evolution Looks like self-evolution is also already a big design component of open-weight LLMs. E.g., the paper says that M2.7 already handles 30 to 50 percent of the daily RL iteration workload, modifies its own scaffold, and completed a 100-round autonomous scaffold optimization cycle with a 30 percent gain on internal evaluations. RyanLee (@RyanLeeMiniMax) Recently, we took time to consolidate all of the work behind M2 and published it here: our M2 paper on arXiv It’s been just over six months since we first open-sourced M2 on December 23 last year. During that time, a number of our ideas and systems have been broadly adopted by the open-source community — including CISPO, Forge RL System, Self-Evolution. Over the past six months, we’ve felt incredible enthusiasm from the open-source community. Nearly every model release reached the #1 spot on the Hugging Face leaderboard. Now it’s time for a new chapter. We’re getting ready for M3. MSA paper is on the road. arxiv.org/abs/2605.26494 — https://nitter.net/RyanLeeMiniMax/status/2059470969249608089#m

Lifespan vs. Victories Building something world-historic requires radical sacrifice. Reject the Comfort of "Quiet Quitting." If you are operating in a hyper-growth environment and your days off happen to be Saturday and Sunday every single week, you are quiet quitting. idees.text_fr: Voici une histoire et une auto-réflexion sur la question de savoir si l'IA me rend vraiment plus productif Hier matin, j'ai trouvé un moyen de compléter la nouvelle approche HVM, qui est beaucoup plus rapide qu'auparavant. J'ai passé quelques heures à écrire un cahier des charges, puis j'ai utilisé Opus pour l'implémenter. Environ 3k lignes de code C plus tard, tout a fonctionné et les performances étaient incroyables : 5 fois plus rapides que HVM4 (stable à ~10x maintenant). Donc, en une journée, j'avais surpassé HVM4. Incroyable. Je n'aurais jamais implémenté ça aussi vite manuellement. Maintenant, entrez aujourd'hui. Je veux transformer ça en une vraie chose, mais je n'ai pas complètement lu les 3k lignes. Alors, comment puis-je lui faire confiance ? J'ai passé toute la journée à auditer le code. Avec l'IA. Plusieurs bugs trouvés, la plupart mineurs comme oublier de collect() un argument. Mais alors je tombe sur ça : λ{ inl: 1 ; inr: 1 } C'était un test. Mais attendez. Ceci correspond à inl/inr. Donc les branches devraient recevoir la valeur de l'Either. Mais c'étaient des nombres à la place. Les nombres ne sont pas des fonctions. Cela n'a aucun sens. Alors pourquoi est-ce un test ? Puis il m'a frappé. L'IA a complètement mal compris comment fonctionnent les arités des fonctions. Elle a littéralement supposé sans aucune raison que HVM5 était censé gérer des fonctions sous/sur-appliquées. Sans aucune raison. Je n'ai jamais écrit ça. Elle n'a jamais demandé non plus. Elle s'est juste dit "HVM est étrange à certains égards, c'est peut-être l'un d'eux..." - et ensuite elle a implémenté un système massif pour gérer des cas qui ne devraient même pas se produire en premier lieu. Et tout ce code est évidemment faux car il ne devrait même pas exister. C'est faux. C'est des dégâts. Et c'est là. Mais ce n'est pas trop grave non plus. J'ai juste dit à Opus qu'elle avait tort. Peut-être pas poliment. Et elle l'a résolu très bien. Mais alors cela soulève la question. J'ai passé ~20 heures sur ce fichier, et ce n'est TOUJOURS pas fini. Je suis passé de 0 à 95% dans les 5 premières heures. Pourtant, 15 heures plus tard, ce n'est toujours pas 100%. Je suppose que c'est le véritable effet de l'utilisation de l'IA. Si j'avais écrit le fichier C manuellement ces deux derniers jours, ne serais-je pas plus loin que là où j'en suis *maintenant* ? Sûrement, la première version aurait pris beaucoup plus de temps à descendre. Mais quand j'aurais fini d'écrire tout ce code, il n'y aurait zéro, littéralement zéro merde retardée. Et le pire, c'est que : je ne connais pas le nombre de merdes retardées restantes, mais j'ai peur qu'il soit >0. Donc si je dois tout lire, tout vérifier pour m'assurer qu'il n'y a pas de merde retardée... qu'ai-je réalisé en utilisant l'IA, autre que cette anticipation de dopamine ?
idees.text_original: Just saving this here to document a story and as a self reflection on whether AI is really making me more productive Yesterday morning I found a way to complete the new HVM approach, that is much faster than before. I spent a few hours writing a spec, and then used Opus to implement. About 3k lines of C code later, everything worked and performance was incredible: 5x faster than HVM4 (stable at ~10x now). So, in one day I had outclassed HVM4. Incredible. I'd never have implemented that so fast manually. Now, enter today. I want to turn this into a real thing, but I haven't fully read the 3k lines yet. So, how do I trust it? I spent the whole day auditing the code. With AI. Several bugs found, most minor like forgetting to collect() some argument. But then I stumble upon this: λ{ inl: 1 ; inr: 1 } This was a test. But wait. This is matching on inl/inr. So the branches should receive the value of the Either. But they were numbers instead. Numbers aren't functions. This makes no sense. So why this is a test? It then stuck me. The AI completely misunderstood how function arities work. It literally assumed for no good reason that HVM5 was supposed to handle under/over-applied functions. For no good reason. I never wrote that. It never asked either. It just kinda thought "HVM is weird in some aspects, this might be one of them..." - and then it went on to implement a massive system to handle cases that should never happen to begin with. And all of that code is obviously wrong because it should not even exist. It is wrong. It is damage. And it is there. But it isn't too bad either. I just told Opus that it was wrong. Perhaps not so politely. And it solved it just fine. But then this begs the question. I spent ~20 hours in this file, and it is STILL not done. I went from 0 to 95% in the first 5 hours. Yet, 15 hours later, it is still not 100%. I suppose that is the real effect of using AI. If I had just written the C file manually in the last two days, would I not be further than where I am *right now*? Surely, the first version would have taken much longer to drop. But when I'd finish writing all that code, there would be zero, literally zero retarded shit. And, just today, I caught 5 or 6 retarded shit. And the worst part is: I don't know what the number of retarded shit left is, but I'm afraid it is >0. outils.text_fr: llama.cpp a maintenant un site officiel : llama.app Notre objectif est de rendre l'IA locale accessible à tous, et l'amélioration de l'expérience utilisateur en est une grande partie. Sur la nouvelle page d'accueil, vous trouverez un installateur multiplateforme en une seule ligne. L'installation fournit un point d'entrée `llama` unifié que vous pouvez utiliser pour exécuter/servir des modèles et interagir avec des applications d'agents tierces. Bien qu'orientée vers une expérience utilisateur simplifiée, la nouvelle application `llama` fournit également toutes les fonctionnalités avancées des outils llama.cpp existants avec lesquels les utilisateurs expérimentés sont déjà familiers. Notez également que tous les modèles GGUF que vous pourriez avoir déjà téléchargés avec llama.cpp par le passé seront automatiquement disponibles sans avoir à les télécharger à nouveau (ils sont stockés dans le cache HF commun sur votre machine). Nous avons de nombreuses améliorations en préparation, tant au niveau de l'UX qu'au niveau du moteur, et nous prévoyons de livrer progressivement de nouvelles choses dans les mois à venir. L'un des principaux axes sera l'intégration transparente avec des agents locaux (tels que Pi). En attendant, nous continuerons à écouter les commentaires de la communauté et à nous adapter en conséquence, alors continuez à nous faire savoir ce que vous pensez et ce dont vous avez besoin.
outils.text_original: llama.cpp now has an official website: llama.app Our goal is to make local AI accessible to everyone, and improving the user experience is a big part of that. On the new landing page you’ll find a single-line cross-platform installer. The installation provides a single unified `llama` entrypoint which you can use to run/serve models and interface with 3rd-party agentic applications. While oriented towards simplified user experience, the new `llama` application also provides all the advanced functionality of the existing llama.cpp tooling with which experienced users are already familiar. Also note that all GGUF models that you might have already downloaded with llama.cpp in the past will be automatically available to use without downloading again (they are stored in the common HF cache on your machine). We have many improvements in the pipeline both at the UX and at the engine level and we plan to iteratively ship new things over the coming months. One of the main focuses will be seamless integration with local-friendly 3rd-party agents (such as Pi). In the meantime, we’ll continue to listen for feedback from the community and adjust accordingly, so keep letting us know what you think and need.
outils.decryptage: llama.cpp, un outil populaire pour faire fonctionner l'IA localement, lance un nouveau site web et un installateur simplifié pour rendre l'IA plus accessible à tous.

outils.text_fr: aujourd'hui a été une journée massive pour l'ingénierie des protéines. esmfold2 est sorti - la prochaine génération de la série esm, entièrement ouverte sur @huggingscience . 1,1 milliard de structures prédites, 6,8 milliards de séquences. 800 millions d'entrées de plus que la base alphafold, et surpasserait alphafold3 sur les complexes protéiques, y compris la liaison anticorps-antigène. à côté : le nouvel atlas esm. une expansion énorme de l'espace protéique connu, riche en séquences métagénomiques provenant du sol, de l'océan et des parties de la biologie les moins caractérisées (jusqu'à maintenant !!) et si cela ne suffisait pas, litefold a sorti le fineweb des protéines, donc chaque base de données majeure de protéines (pdb inclus) agrégée, nettoyée et prête à l'emploi en un seul endroit. ce sont les sorties qui font avancer tout le domaine, et le rythme de la science ouverte est actuellement presque donnant le mal de mer, le tout sur huggingscience.co (et bien sûr @huggingface )
outils.text_original: today was a massive day for protein engineering. esmfold2 dropped—next gen of the esm series, fully open on @huggingscience . 1.1 billion predicted structures, 6.8 billion sequences. 800m more entries than the alphafold db, and reportedly edging out alphafold3 on protein complexes, including antibody–antigen binding. alongside it: the new esm atlas. a huge expansion of known protein space, heavy on metagenomic sequences from soil, ocean, and the parts of biology that have been least characterised (until now!!) and if that weren't enough, litefold dropped the fineweb of proteins, so every major protein database (pdb included) aggregated, cleaned, and made plug-and-play in one place. these are the releases that push the whole field forward, and the pace of open science right now is almost motion-sickness inducing all of it on huggingscience.co (and ofc @huggingface )
outils.decryptage: Une vague de nouvelles découvertes open-source en bio-informatique (protéines, ADN) révolutionne la recherche, rendant des données et outils puissants accessibles à tous.
